units.text: ⟦0⟧3.2 Character Classes and Bracket Expressions⟦1⟧
units.sourceHTML: 3.2 Character Classes and Bracket Expressions

units.text: A ⟦0⟧bracket expression⟦1⟧ is a list of characters enclosed by ‘⟦2⟧’ and ‘⟦3⟧’. It matches any single character in that list. If the first character of the list is the caret ‘⟦4⟧’, then it matches any character ⟦5⟧not⟦6⟧ in the list, and it is unspecified whether it matches an encoding error. For example, the regular expression ‘⟦7⟧’ matches any single digit, whereas ‘⟦8⟧’ matches any single character that is not an opening or closing parenthesis, and might or might not match an encoding error.
units.sourceHTML: A bracket expression is a list of characters enclosed by ‘[’ and ‘]’. It matches any single character in that list. If the first character of the list is the caret ‘^’, then it matches any character not in the list, and it is unspecified whether it matches an encoding error. For example, the regular expression ‘[0123456789]’ matches any single digit, whereas ‘[^()]’ matches any single character that is not an opening or closing parenthesis, and might or might not match an encoding error.

units.text: Within a bracket expression, a ⟦0⟧range expression⟦1⟧ consists of two characters separated by a hyphen. In the default C locale, it matches any single character that appears between the two characters in ASCII order, inclusive. For example, ‘⟦2⟧’ is equivalent to ‘⟦3⟧’. In other locales the behavior is unspecified: ‘⟦4⟧’ might be equivalent to ‘⟦5⟧’ or ‘⟦6⟧’ or some other bracket expression, or it might fail to match any character, or the set of characters that it matches might be erratic, or it might be invalid. To obtain the traditional interpretation of bracket expressions, you can use the ‘⟦7⟧’ locale by setting the ⟦8⟧ environment variable to the value ‘⟦9⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Within a bracket expression, a range expression consists of two characters separated by a hyphen. In the default C locale, it matches any single character that appears between the two characters in ASCII order, inclusive. For example, ‘[a-d]’ is equivalent to ‘[abcd]’. In other locales the behavior is unspecified: ‘[a-d]’ might be equivalent to ‘[abcd]’ or ‘[aBbCcDd]’ or some other bracket expression, or it might fail to match any character, or the set of characters that it matches might be erratic, or it might be invalid. To obtain the traditional interpretation of bracket expressions, you can use the ‘C’ locale by setting the LC_ALL environment variable to the value ‘C’.

units.text: Finally, certain named classes of characters are predefined within bracket expressions, as follows. Their interpretation depends on the ⟦0⟧ locale; for example, ‘⟦1⟧’ means the character class of numbers and letters in the current locale.
units.sourceHTML: Finally, certain named classes of characters are predefined within bracket expressions, as follows. Their interpretation depends on the LC_CTYPE locale; for example, ‘[[:alnum:]]’ means the character class of numbers and letters in the current locale.

units.text: Alphanumeric characters: ‘⟦0⟧’ and ‘⟦1⟧’; in the ‘⟦2⟧’ locale and ASCII character encoding, this is the same as ‘⟦3⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Alphanumeric characters: ‘[:alpha:]’ and ‘[:digit:]’; in the ‘C’ locale and ASCII character encoding, this is the same as ‘[0-9A-Za-z]’.

units.text: Alphabetic characters: ‘⟦0⟧’ and ‘⟦1⟧’; in the ‘⟦2⟧’ locale and ASCII character encoding, this is the same as ‘⟦3⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Alphabetic characters: ‘[:lower:]’ and ‘[:upper:]’; in the ‘C’ locale and ASCII character encoding, this is the same as ‘[A-Za-z]’.

units.text: Blank characters: space and tab.
units.sourceHTML: Blank characters: space and tab.

units.text: Control characters. In ASCII, these characters have octal codes 000 through 037, and 177 (DEL). In other character sets, these are the equivalent characters, if any.
units.sourceHTML: Control characters. In ASCII, these characters have octal codes 000 through 037, and 177 (DEL). In other character sets, these are the equivalent characters, if any.

units.sourceHTML: Graphical characters: ‘[:alnum:]’ and ‘[:punct:]’.

units.text: Note that the brackets in these class names are part of the symbolic names, and must be included in addition to the brackets delimiting the bracket expression.
units.sourceHTML: Note that the brackets in these class names are part of the symbolic names, and must be included in addition to the brackets delimiting the bracket expression.

units.text: If you mistakenly omit the outer brackets, and search for say, ‘⟦0⟧’, GNU ⟦1⟧ prints a diagnostic and exits with status 2, on the assumption that you did not intend to search for the regular expression ‘⟦2⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: If you mistakenly omit the outer brackets, and search for say, ‘[:upper:]’, GNU grep prints a diagnostic and exits with status 2, on the assumption that you did not intend to search for the regular expression ‘[:epru]’.

units.text: Special characters lose their special meaning inside bracket expressions.
